summary: Describes the usage of BGP in the Internet. It was on the standards track and is now historic. It was replaced by RFC 1655.

eli5.summary: It explains how to use BGP in the real Internet. It has been replaced.

questions: how is bgp used in the internet
how does bgp prevent routing loops
subtitle: How the Border Gateway Protocol is deployed and used across the Internet.

tldr.problem: The Internet is a collection of independent networks called Autonomous Systems that need to exchange routing information across their boundaries while respecting administrative policies and avoiding routing loops.
tldr.mechanism: BGP allows border gateways of different Autonomous Systems to advertise the complete path to each network, enabling each AS to enforce its own routing policies and detect loops by checking if its own AS number appears in the path.
tldr.outcome: BGP enables each network to control how traffic flows through it, prevent routing loops, and build a flexible, policy-based Internet backbone. It became the de facto inter-domain routing protocol.

facts.label: AS connection requirement
facts.value: BGP speakers must share a network with border gateways

facts.label: AS path role
facts.value: Prevents routing loops and enables policy decisions

facts.label: Primary topology types
facts.value: Stub, multihomed, and transit Autonomous Systems

today: RFC 1268 is now Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 1655. It describes BGP-3, which became the foundation for modern BGP deployments. The core concepts of policy-based routing and AS-path-based loop detection remain central to Internet routing architecture today, though subsequent RFCs (like RFC 4271 for BGP-4) have extended and refined the protocol.

sections.title: Introduction to BGP in the Internet
sections.content:
BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the protocol Autonomous Systems use to exchange routing information across the Internet. An Autonomous System is a set of networks under a single organization, using interior routing protocols internally and BGP to talk to other organizations.

BGP differs from earlier routing protocols by carrying the full path of Autonomous Systems that a route has traversed. This allows each AS to detect loops (by refusing routes that list its own AS number) and make policy decisions (by choosing which routes to accept or advertise based on business relationships).
sections.eli5: Each post office (AS) tells neighbors where mail can go and what it learned from other post offices. If a route comes back that visited your post office already, you know it's a loop.

sections.title: Autonomous Systems and Topologies
sections.content:
The Internet topology can be modeled as a graph where nodes are Autonomous Systems and edges are BGP connections. BGP defines three types of ASes: stub ASes (connected to only one other AS), multihomed ASes (connected to multiple ASes but unwilling to carry transit traffic), and transit ASes (designed to carry traffic between other ASes).

BGP does not require special topologies; it works with arbitrary interconnections because the full AS path prevents routing loops. This flexibility is one of BGP's key strengths, allowing the Internet to grow without needing a hierarchical structure.
sections.eli5: Some post offices are small branches (stub), some are medium offices connected to several others but busy with their own mail (multihomed), and some are big hubs that relay mail between many offices (transit).

sections.title: BGP Peers and Communication
sections.content:
Routers that communicate directly via BGP are called BGP neighbors or peers. When neighbors are in the same AS, this is called Internal BGP (IBGP); when in different ASes, it is External BGP (EBGP). All BGP speakers within an AS must present a consistent view of the AS to the outside world.

BGP requires that EBGP neighbors share a common network and send control messages directly over it. This prevents the need for the sending AS to route BGP messages through another AS, which would invalidate the AS path information.
sections.eli5: Neighbors talk directly if they're next to each other. Inside a post office, different clerks coordinate (IBGP). Between post offices, the main managers talk (EBGP).

sections.title: Policies and Path Selection
sections.content:
BGP allows each AS to enforce routing policies by controlling which routes it advertises and which ones it accepts. For example, a multihomed AS can refuse to advertise routes learned from one neighbor to another neighbor, effectively refusing to carry transit traffic between them.

When multiple paths to a destination exist, BGP speakers evaluate them using criteria like AS count (shorter is better), policy constraints, knowledge of specific ASes' performance characteristics, path origin, and link stability. Each AS assigns these criteria through configuration, allowing sophisticated economic and performance optimization.
sections.eli5: Each post office decides who it will take mail from and send mail to. 'I'll take mail from my friend Bob but won't send him stuff to forward to Carol because they had an argument.'

sections.title: Interaction with Interior Routing
sections.content:
Within an AS, interior gateway protocols (IGPs) like OSPF or RIP handle routing to destinations inside the network. BGP learns routes from EBGP, but interior routers need to know how to reach the exit points through which those external routes are reachable.

This requires coordination: BGP information must be distributed internally before border gateways advertise those routes externally. If this synchronization fails, packets can be black-holed (sent to an exit point that interior routers cannot reach). The RFC describes techniques like using the IGP itself to distribute BGP information, tagging routes with their exit point, or encapsulating transit traffic to exit points.
sections.eli5: Inside the post office, mail carriers need to know which exit door to use for each outside delivery. The information from neighbors (BGP) must match which exits are actually available (IGP) before we promise neighbors we can deliver there.
